title: Daughter of God (Leviticus Rabbah 1:3)
hook: midrash names Pharaoh's daughter Bityah, daughter of God, for saving a child not her own
tomorrow: four kids ask about the seder. why do they get four answers?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miriam argued her father out of despair and stood by the river to see her hope through. Miriam believed. Today, the woman on the other side of that river.
screen: `MIRIAM BELIEVED.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Somewhere on a family tree there is often a name nobody can place: a great-aunt from somewhere else, a surname that doesn't match. The Bible has one like that. Deep in a list of names in Chronicles, inside the family of Judah, sits a woman called Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh. Pharaoh's daughter, in an Israelite family tree, with a Hebrew name. Who is she, and how did she get there?
screen: `A NAME NOBODY CAN PLACE.` → `PHARAOH'S DAUGHTER, IN JUDAH'S LIST.` → `WITH A HEBREW NAME?`

segments.voice: The rabbis answer with the princess from Exodus, the one who drew the baby Moses out of the Nile. The Torah never tells us her name. But Leviticus Rabbah reads Chronicles and hears it: Bityah, bat-Yah, daughter of God. And it gives God's reason in one balanced line. Moses was not your son, and you called him your son. You are not My daughter, and I call you My daughter. Look at the trade. She gave a child who wasn't hers a name and a home; heaven gives her a name and a family. The Torah's own words back her up: when the child grew, "he became her son." Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud learns from Bityah that whoever raises someone else's child, the text counts it as if they had given birth. So the puzzle in Chronicles solves itself. The daughter of the king who ordered the decree is written into Judah's family, because she opened a basket, heard a baby crying, and decided this child was hers to protect. She doesn't switch sides by argument. She switches by caring. Some readers see in her every grown-up who chooses a child who isn't theirs: foster parents, adoptive parents, a teacher, the neighbor who keeps an eye out.
screen: `THE PRINCESS AT THE NILE.` · `BAT-YAH: DAUGHTER OF GOD.` · `NOT YOUR SON. NOT MY DAUGHTER.` · `RAISING IS LIKE GIVING BIRTH.` · then, large: `DAUGHTER OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Name one child who isn't yours who could use a grown-up's attention: a niece, a younger teammate, a neighbor's kid, a student. Choose one small, appropriate thing you could do for them this week, with their parents' okay, like help with homework or a word of encouragement. Picture yourself doing it, and decide when.
screen: `ONE CHILD, NOT YOURS.` · `ONE SMALL THING.` · `DECIDE WHEN.`

segments.voice: Bityah: the name the midrash gives Pharaoh's daughter, heard as daughter of God, for raising a child who wasn't hers.
Daughter of God: what heaven calls the one who loves a child not her own. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish law and custom honor those who raise children not born to them; the Talmud's teaching that raising an orphan is like giving birth is learned from Bityah.

chat.meaning: Moses wasn't her son, yet she called him her son; so God calls her My daughter. Caring for a child not your own is honored.

notes: Leviticus Rabbah 1:3 paraphrased; the reading of Bityah as bat-Yah (daughter of God) is the midrash's own wordplay, not a lexicon etymology. Confirm.
1 Chronicles 4:18 (Bithiah in Judah's genealogy) paraphrased; confirm the placement 'inside the family of Judah'.
Exodus 2:10 quoted from JPS 1917 ('he became her son'); confirm.
Sanhedrin 19b paraphrased ('as if they had given birth'); confirm the derivation from Bityah.
'Some readers see in her every grown-up who chooses a child' is framed as a reading, not a claim about the tradition.
